• Apply BODMAS: 168 ÷ 42 = 4; 14 × 9 = 126.

 

• 4 − 126 + 207 = −122 + 207 = 85.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option D.

 

SHORT TRICK

 

• Rewrite the whole expression with the new (swapped) symbols first before doing any arithmetic — attempting to swap 'on the fly' while calculating is a common source of errors.

 

NOTE

 

• Always perform all multiplications/divisions (left to right) before additions/subtractions (left to right), exactly as per BODMAS, even after symbol substitution.

question:
Seven boxes A, B, C, D, E, F and G are kept one over the other but not necessarily in the same order.

No box is kept above D. Only three boxes are kept between D and F. Only one box is kept between G and E. E is kept immediately above F. Only four boxes are kept between G and A. C is kept at some place above B.

How many boxes are kept above C?
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option A i.e. 2.

 

GIVEN

 

• 7 boxes A-G stacked vertically (position 1 = bottom, position 7 = top), with the clue relationships described above.

 

SOLUTION

 

• 'No box is kept above D' ⇒ D is at the top: D = 7.

 

• 'Only three boxes between D and F' ⇒ D and F are 4 positions apart ⇒ F = 7 − 4 = 3.

 

• 'E is kept immediately above F' ⇒ E = F + 1 = 4.

 

• 'Only one box between G and E' ⇒ G is 2 positions from E ⇒ G = 4+2 = 6 or G = 4−2 = 2 (to be checked against the next clue).

 

• 'Only four boxes between G and A' ⇒ |G − A| = 5. If G = 6, A = 1 (valid, since 6−5=1). If G = 2, A would need to be −3 or 7 (7 already taken by D) — invalid. So G = 6, A = 1.

question:
Read the given statements and conclusions carefully. Assuming that the information given in the statements is true, even if it appears to be at variance with commonly known facts, decide which of the given conclusions logically follow(s) from the statements.

Statements:

All kiwis are bananas.

All bananas are mangoes.

Conclusions:

(I): All kiwis are mangoes.

(II): Some mangoes are bananas.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option A i.e. Both conclusions (I) and (II) follow.

 

GIVEN

 

• Statements: All kiwis are bananas (A-type). All bananas are mangoes (A-type).

 

SOLUTION

 

• Since all kiwis are bananas, and all bananas are mangoes, by the transitive chain of the syllogism (A + A = A pattern), it follows that all kiwis are mangoes — this is exactly Conclusion (I), so it follows.

 

• Since 'All bananas are mangoes' is given as true, it automatically also means that some mangoes are bananas (an 'All A are B' statement always implies 'Some B are A', by conversion) — this is exactly Conclusion (II), so it also follows.

 

• Both conclusions are therefore valid.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option A.

 

SHORT TRICK

 

• 'All A are B' + 'All B are C' always gives the valid conclusion 'All A are C' (chain/transitive rule); and any 'All X are Y' statement always converts to a valid 'Some Y are X'.

 

NOTE

 

• Don't be influenced by the real-world truth of the statements (kiwis are not literally bananas) — in syllogisms, statements are always taken as true exactly as given.

question:
In a certain code language,

'A + B' means 'A is the father of B'

'A − B' means 'A is the mother of B'

'A * B' means 'A is the sister of B'

'A ÷ B' means 'A is the wife of B'

Based on the above, how is X related to Q if 'X ÷ Y + Z * P − Q'?
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option D i.e. Mother's mother.

 

GIVEN

 

• Code: '+' = father of, '−' = mother of, '*' = sister of, '÷' = wife of. Expression: X ÷ Y + Z * P − Q.

 

SOLUTION

 

• X ÷ Y: X is the wife of Y.

 

• Y + Z: Y is the father of Z. Since X is Y's wife, X is also Z's mother (X and Y are Z's parents).

 

• Z * P: Z is the sister of P, so Z and P are siblings — both children of X and Y.

 

• P − Q: P is the mother of Q.

 

• Since X is P's mother, and P is Q's mother, X is the mother of P, who is the mother of Q — so X is Q's maternal grandmother, i.e. mother's mother.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option D.

 

SHORT TRICK

 

• Decode the family-tree chain one relation at a time from left to right, drawing a quick family tree (X-Y as a couple, their children Z & P, and P's child Q) — this makes the final generational relation immediately visible.

 

NOTE

 

• Always identify who forms a couple (via '÷', wife-of) and who are their joint children (via '+'/'−') before deriving further downstream relations.

SOLUTION

 

• Fix X at position 0 (clockwise numbering 0-6). 'A sits third to the left of X' ⇒ A is 3 steps anticlockwise from X, so A = 0 − 3 = 4 (mod 7).

 

• 'Only one person between X and C, counted from the left of C' ⇒ X is 2 steps anticlockwise from C, i.e. X = C − 2, so C = X + 2 = 2.

 

• Remaining positions {1, 3, 5, 6} are for B, D, W, Y. 'Only two people between B and W, counted from the right of W' ⇒ B = W + 3 (mod 7). Testing W = 3 gives B = 6 (both available) — this works; testing W = 5 gives B = 1, but then D (needing to be adjacent to B) would have no valid neighbouring seat left, so it is rejected.

 

• With W = 3, B = 6, the last two positions {1, 5} remain for D and Y. 'D is an immediate neighbour of B(6)': B's neighbours are positions 5 and 0(X, already taken), so D must be position 5, leaving Y = 1.

 

• Final clockwise order: X(0), Y(1), C(2), W(3), A(4), D(5), B(6).

 

• 'Third to the right of Y': Y = 1, moving clockwise 3 steps: 1+3 = 4 = A.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option A.

 

SHORT TRICK

 

• For circular seating facing the centre, treat 'right' as clockwise and 'left' as anticlockwise consistently; convert every 'N people between P and Q, counted from left/right of P' clue into a direct positional equation (Q = P ± (N+1)) to solve step by step.

 

NOTE

 

• When a 'between' clue yields two possible positions, test each against the remaining adjacency/neighbour clues to eliminate the invalid one, as done here for W.
